title: Design exercise: notifications
summary: A classic design exercise: a shared notification service for push, email and SMS with preferences, quiet hours, provider failover and no duplicates. The reference answer uses an idempotency key per (event, user, channel), one durable queue per channel and priority class, adapters behind circuit breakers with a secondary provider, collapse identifiers at the provider, and a delivery status store; the design-doc frame follows the outline's worked example.

exercise.prompt: Design a notification service that several product teams use to send push, email and SMS to users. A user must see each event once, on the channels they allow and not during their quiet hours; a provider outage must not stop delivery; the sending team must be able to ask what happened to a notification.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: An API for internal teams to send a notification for an event to a user on one or more channels; per-user preferences and quiet hours; templates per team.
Delivery status by notification id; provider failover; retries without duplicates.
20 million users; 50 million notifications per day.
70 percent push, 25 percent email, 5 percent SMS.
Peak 10 times the daily average; five sending teams today, more later.
derive the per-second rates per channel and the queue sizes yourself
Push handed to the provider within 5 s at p95; email within 60 s; SMS within 30 s; provider failover within 60 s of detection.
At-least-once delivery to the provider with deduplication so a user sees one message per event; 99.9 percent availability of the send API.
Marketing campaigns and audience selection, an in-app inbox, analytics beyond delivery status, exactly-once delivery across providers (not possible end to end).

clarifying_questions.a: The sending team proposes channels per event type; the user's preferences and quiet hours filter them; the service never adds a channel the team did not ask for.

clarifying_questions.q: What is the duplicate we must prevent?
clarifying_questions.a: The same event sent twice by a retrying caller, and the same queued notification processed twice by a retrying consumer. The same event sent with two different event ids by the caller is not caught, and the API contract says so.
Push and SMS are held until the window ends (or dropped if the event expires); email is sent, since it does not wake anyone (assumption; a product decision the doc must state).
Two: transactional (security codes, receipts) which ignores quiet hours and rate limits, and informational which honours both.

clarifying_questions.q: How long is delivery status kept?
clarifying_questions.a: 90 days (assumption), queryable by notification id and by user.
Phone numbers and device tokens only inside the adapter boundary and the status store, encrypted at rest; teams send user ids, never addresses.

blocks.text: One API in front of a preference lookup, one durable queue per channel and priority class (six queues) with competing consumers, provider adapters behind circuit breakers with a secondary provider each, a delivery status store written from provider callbacks, and a dead-letter queue with an operator view. The channel queues are separate because the channels have different latency targets and different providers; a shared queue would let an SMS backlog delay push. Fan-out of one event to several channels happens at the API, the way a publish-subscribe topic fans one message out to several queues.

blocks.legend: Boxes are containers, the outer frame is the system boundary, hexagons are external systems, double brackets are queues; each queue node stands for two queues, one per priority class, and the dotted edges carry messages whose retries are exhausted.

blocks.text: The push providers are the two public ones: FCM's architecture page describes an app server handing messages to the FCM backend, which routes them through a platform-level transport layer to the device, and APNs' provider API takes a device token, a priority, an expiry and a collapse identifier per request. The adapter boundary exists so that these two APIs, their tokens and their quirks are seen by one component only.

blocks.text: Teams authenticate with per-team credentials and are rate limited per team. The idempotency key is kept for 24 hours, the lifetime Stripe's API reference gives for its own keys (pruned once they are at least a day old); a caller that retries within that window gets the first result, and the contract says plainly that the same event sent with two different event ids is not caught.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: One informational event for a user who allows push and email, sent during the day.

blocks.title: Validate, decide, enqueue, deliver, record
items: The API validates the request, checks the idempotency key in a 24-hour key store, and returns the stored result if the key is known.

The API reads the user's preferences: push and email enabled, no quiet hours now, under the per-user limit of 10 informational pushes per hour (assumption). SMS was not requested. It renders the templates and writes one Notification per channel in state queued.

The API enqueues one message per channel on that channel's queue and returns the notification ids. Writing the record and enqueueing are made safe by writing the record first and treating a duplicate enqueue as harmless (the consumer deduplicates by notification id).

A push adapter worker takes the message (visibility timeout 30 s), loads the device tokens, and calls the primary push provider with a collapse identifier equal to the event id so that a redelivered or updated notification replaces rather than duplicates on the device (APNs exposes apns-collapse-id on its provider API; the adapter uses each provider's equivalent), and an expiry equal to expires_at.

On success the worker records the attempt and state sent, and deletes the queue message. On a transient failure it retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff and jitter; on a hard failure (invalid token) it marks failed and removes the token.
Provider callbacks (delivered, bounced, unsubscribed) arrive on a webhook, are matched by provider message id, and update the status store; the email adapter maps a bounce to a suppressed address.
A message that exhausts retries on both providers goes to the dead-letter queue with its last error; the operator view lets a team replay or discard it.

blocks.text: The bottleneck is the provider, not the service: each provider has its own rate limits and its own bad days. The adapter keeps a circuit breaker per provider; when the primary's error rate crosses a threshold the breaker opens and traffic shifts to the secondary within the 60 s failover target, with the breaker probing the primary in a half-open state. Adapter workers scale on queue age (oldest message age), not on queue length, because age is the SLI the targets are written in.

blocks.caption: The backlog rules this design takes from the Builders' Library article on queue backlogs.
rows: Separate workloads so one backlog cannot starve another
one queue per channel: an SMS backlog never delays push
Keep one tenant from filling everyone's queue
per-team quotas at the API, and a sidelined queue for a team whose messages keep failing
Drain by age, so fresh urgent work is not stuck behind stale work
the transactional class has its own queue per channel; old informational messages past their expiry are dropped rather than sent late
queue age per channel is the alarm, with the threshold at the channel's target

blocks.text: Preferences are read on every send: 5,800 reads per second at peak against a 20-million-row table is a cache job, cache-aside with a short TTL and invalidation on preference change. Per-user rate limits are token buckets keyed by user and channel in the same cache.

blocks.title: Quiet hours: hold, collapse, release
items: A notification that lands inside the user's quiet hours is stored with a release time and the state held; its expiry is still enforced.
The held set per user is capped (assumption: a handful per channel); when the cap is exceeded the newest wins and the older ones are collapsed, so a user does not wake up to 40 pings.
A scheduler re-enqueues held notifications when the window ends; anything past its expiry is dropped and the status store says so.
Transactional notifications (security codes, receipts) skip the hold entirely; that is what the priority class is for.

blocks.text: Each row names the failure, what the user and the team see, and the mitigation.

rows: breaker opens on error rate; secondary provider takes traffic within 60 s; alert on breaker state

Caller retries with the same event
idempotency key for 24 hours returns the first result
Consumer crashes after the provider call, before the ack
collapse identifier at the provider; status store shows the attempt; the second attempt sees state sent and skips
SMS backlog from a provider incident
its own queue; push and email unaffected; age-based alert; operator can pause the channel

a shared service; the managed product is one provider behind the adapter
shared dedupe and preferences need shared state; provider changes deploy once
one queue with a channel field versus one queue per channel and priority
one per channel and priority class
channel latency targets differ; a backlog must not cross channels
exactly-once attempts versus at-least-once plus collapse and dedupe
at-least-once with idempotency key, status check and collapse id
exactly-once across a provider boundary is not available; collapse makes a rare duplicate harmless on the device

send push, hold SMS and email

silence is also a failure for transactional events; SMS costs money and wakes people; an unknown email preference may be an unsubscribe, and a held email still meets its 60 s target if the outage is short

priority classes enforced during incidents by shedding informational traffic first

blocks.text: At this scale the platform questions are the design: what each team may spend per channel, which class is shed first in an incident, who reviews a template, and where a user's consent and addresses are allowed to live.

L1: A queue per channel with competing consumers, provider adapters, bounded retries with jitter, and an idempotency key for callers.
A delivery status store written from attempts and provider callbacks, and the per-channel rates derived from the assumptions.
The duplicate story stated honestly: what is caught (caller retries, consumer redelivery) and what is not (two event ids for one event).
L2: Preferences and quiet hours with held messages, a release scheduler, collapsing and per-user limits.
Circuit breakers per provider with a secondary provider and a 60 s failover argument, and workers scaled on queue age.
Backlog handling: separate queues per channel and priority, per-team quotas, sidelining of a failing sender, age-based draining.
The preference-service outage default chosen and justified.
L3: The platform questions: quotas and cost per channel per team, priority classes during incidents, template governance, consent and retention.
Why a library per team or a managed product alone does not solve the problem, with the managed product kept as a provider.
The deprecation plan for the teams' existing direct-to-provider code paths, with shadow mode before cutover.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: who chooses channels, what duplicate means, quiet hours, priority classes, status retention, where personal data lives. Say the numbers aloud: 5,800 notifications per second at peak (4,060 push), a 244,000-message push backlog after a 60 s provider stall, about 400 concurrent provider calls in flight.

0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Notification with its idempotency key of (event, user, channel), Preference, DeviceToken and Address inside the adapter boundary, DeliveryStatus, Template; the send and status endpoints.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: API, preference lookup, a queue per channel and priority class, adapters with breakers and secondary providers, status store, dead letter. Say why the queues are separate.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: duplicates and retries (idempotency key, consumer redelivery, collapse identifiers, bounded retries then failover then dead letter), then backlogs and failover (breakers, scaling on age, per-team quotas and sidelining, quiet-hour holds and collapsing).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x platform (quotas, priority shedding, compliance, regions), and the L3 sentence: the product decision hiding in this design is what to do when the preference service is down, and it should be written down before the review.

Context and scope: Five product teams send push, email and SMS from their own code paths with three providers and no shared dedupe; the incidents of the last quarters (duplicate sends after retries, a provider outage with no failover, no quiet hours). Scope: one internal service for all teams; marketing campaigns and an in-app inbox out of scope.

Goals and non-goals: At-least-once delivery with dedupe so the user sees one message per event; failover within 60 s; preferences and quiet hours; status queryable by the sending team. Non-goals: exactly-once across providers, real-time analytics.
Design: This answer fills it: the API with idempotency keys, the preference lookup, one queue per channel and priority, adapters behind breakers, the status store, the dead-letter view.

Alternatives considered: A library per team (no shared dedupe, three deployments of every provider change); one queue for all channels (SMS backlog delays push); a managed product alone (preferences still need our data), kept as a provider.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security: internal API, per-team credentials, personal data only inside the adapter boundary and the status store, encrypted at rest. Observability: queue age per channel, send success by provider, dedupe hit ratio, breaker state; alert on queue age over the channel target. Cost: per-channel unit cost with SMS the driver, budget with the sending team via a quota. Rollout: shadow mode, then one team's push, then all channels; rollback is a config flag per team.

Review questions the doc must answer: What happens to a notification when the preference service is down (stale cache first, then send push, hold SMS and email); how retries are bounded per provider (3 attempts with jitter, then failover, then dead letter); the dedupe key's lifetime (24 h) and the duplicate it does not catch.
